slides.title: Rebuilding Harlow’s operating margin

paragraphs.text: Rebuilding Harlow’s operating margin
Where the margin went, the plan to bring it back toward 3.0% by FY2028, and what to do first
Board of Directors meeting, February 2027
Prepared for Dana Whitfield, Chief Executive Officer
All company data in this document is synthetic benchmark data taken from the briefing pack. Figures are $ millions unless stated.

slides.title: Executive summary: fix promotions, shrink, delivery pricing and loss-making stores rather than cutting store hours, and start with the tested, low-capital moves now

paragraphs.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Executive summary: fix promotions, shrink, delivery pricing and loss-making stores rather than cutting store hours, and start with the tested, low-capital moves now
1  Wages are not the main cause of the decline

Operating margin fell 2.35 pts (3.37% → 1.02%, FY2023–25). Gross margin explains 1.02 pts (promotions −0.70, shrink −0.50, partly offset by private label +0.18) and e-commerce fulfillment 0.84 pts. Store labor explains only 0.30 pts, because fewer hours per $ of sales (−6%) absorbed most of the +9.4% wage rise.
2  Management’s draft (cut hours 8%, freeze e-commerce) would not reach the target

The $14.5M saving would probably shrink to ~$4.5M, because thinly staffed stores run 3.1% shrink against 2.3% in the best-staffed. That leaves FY2026 operating income near the $20M covenant and the FY2028 margin at about 1–1.5%. The freeze also locks in an e-commerce loss of $10.4M a year.
3  Instead, pull four groups of levers worth ~$29M a year by FY2028

Commercial (cut loss-making promotions, rebuild vendor funding, grow private label) $13.5M · store operations (cut shrink, reshape rather than cut labor) $6.4M · re-price home delivery, which is kept $2.5M · exit the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA $6.6M.
4  This protects the covenant but reaches 3.0% only if upside lands

Base case: FY2026 operating income $24.8M (covenant $20M) and FY2028 margin 2.65%, after absorbing a $6.8M wage step. Reaching 3.0% needs $4.9M more, about one-third of the $15M upside we identified. Capital needed: ~$20M of the $25M envelope.
5  What to do first (next 90 days)

Roll out the tested delivery fee chain-wide. Drop the money-losing promotions and make vendor co-funding a condition of every event. Cancel the blanket hours cut and move hours to produce and receiving. Serve notice on the six expiring leases. Rebid the delivery contract instead of accepting +3%.
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. FY = fiscal year ending January. Base case = risk-adjusted plan; all lever values are annual run-rates.

slides.title: We started from a hypothesis and tested it. Three of six conditions held fully and two partly, and the evidence changed the answer in three ways

paragraphs.text: APPROACH
We started from a hypothesis and tested it. Three of six conditions held fully and two partly, and the evidence changed the answer in three ways

Initial hypothesis (stated at kick-off): the decline is driven by promotions, shrink and loss-making delivery, not wages. Fixing those, rather than cutting store hours, gets Harlow back to 3.0% by FY2028.

data: What would have to be true
1. Wages are a minor driver of the decline
Labor = 0.30 of 2.35 pts (13%). Wage +9.4%, hours per $1,000 of sales −6.0%
2. Gross-margin erosion comes from Harlow’s own choices
Promo mix −0.70 + shrink −0.50 + private label +0.18 = −1.02 pts, which matches the actual change exactly
3. Promotions can be cut back without losing core shoppers
38% of events lose money; price perception worsened anyway (33% → 41% "more expensive"). But stores near ValuMart run −4.2% comps
Partly: keep value investment in ValuMart trade areas
4. Delivery is the e-commerce problem and can be fixed while keeping it
Delivered order −$12.34, click-and-collect −$1.64. The fee test recovers ~$2.5M, but delivery still loses ~$9 an order
Partly: re-pricing closes only ~¼ of the loss
Shrink 3.1% in the least-staffed quartile vs 2.3% in the most-staffed; managers report skipped checks (correlation, not proven cause)
6. The fixes reach 3.0% within $25M and keep the covenant
Covenant holds in the base case ($24.8M). FY2028 margin 2.65%, so 3.0% needs upside

paragraphs.text: How the answer changed: (a) all nine loss-making stores are now in the core plan, not only those with expiring leases; (b) labor moved from "do not touch" to "reshape": −2% net hours, taken from the most heavily staffed stores; (c) 3.0% is presented honestly as base case 2.65% plus a named stretch plan, not as a certainty.
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Verdict colours: green = supported; amber = partly supported; red = not supported on the base case.

slides.title: Gross margin (1.02 pts) and e-commerce fulfillment (0.84 pts) explain nearly 80% of the 2.35-pt margin decline. Store labor explains 0.30 pts

paragraphs.text: 1  WHY MARGIN FELL
Gross margin (1.02 pts) and e-commerce fulfillment (0.84 pts) explain nearly 80% of the 2.35-pt margin decline. Store labor explains 0.30 pts
Operating margin bridge, FY2023 → FY2025, percentage points of sales
What the bridge says
•  Promotions are the largest single driver. Promo share rose 24% → 29% of sales at a 14-pt lower margin: −0.70 pts (≈ $10.5M)
•  E-commerce fulfillment grew from $5.2M to $18.1M as orders tripled: −0.84 pts (≈ $12.6M)
•  Store labor added only 0.30 pts (≈ $4.5M), and occupancy 0.20 pts
•  Other SG&A held at 4.7% of sales
•  Wages are a real cost pressure but not the main cause: 87% of the decline lies elsewhere
Gross margin: −1.02 pts

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Each line is its % of sales in FY2025 minus FY2023. Gross-margin split: promo-share change × 14-pt margin gap; private-label share change × 12-pt premium; shrink change 1:1. The three reconcile exactly to the −1.02-pt gross-margin change.

slides.title: Deeper promotions have not defended traffic. 38% of events lose money and more shoppers now see Harlow as expensive

paragraphs.text: 1  WHY MARGIN FELL
Deeper promotions have not defended traffic. 38% of events lose money and more shoppers now see Harlow as expensive
Promotional sales, % of sales
Vendor funding of promo markdowns
Shoppers who say Harlow is "more expensive"
More promotion, worse price image
A large share of the spend destroys value
Shoppers come for fresh and convenience
Category managers deepened promotions "to defend traffic against ValuMart". Yet stores within 3 miles of a ValuMart still ran −4.2% comps (vs +1.1%), and the "expensive" score rose 8 pts.
38% of FY2025 events lost money even after counting their extra units. Harlow also now funds 54% of markdowns itself, up from 45%.
The top reasons to shop Harlow are fresh produce (58%) and convenience (44%), not price. Money is better spent on fresh quality and value private label than on deep national-brand discounts.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Promotional margin gap (14 pts) and private-label premium (12 pts) unchanged over the period. Price-perception survey n = 3,100.

slides.title: Wage inflation was largely offset by productivity, and further hour cuts would raise shrink. The 8% cut nets ~$4.5M, not $14.5M

paragraphs.text: 1  WHY MARGIN FELL
Wage inflation was largely offset by productivity, and further hour cuts would raise shrink. The 8% cut nets ~$4.5M, not $14.5M
The wage rise was mostly absorbed by fewer hours per $ of sales
Shrink by store labor intensity, FY2025, % of sales
Stores ranked by labor hours per $1,000 of sales
Management’s 8% hours cut: what it would really save, $M a year
Implication
•  Shrink falls steeply from Q1 to Q2 (0.4 pt) but barely from Q3 to Q4 (0.1 pt). Hours matter most in thinly staffed stores
•  Managers in Q1 stores report skipping produce rotation and receiving checks on busy days. Produce waste is 45% of shrink
•  Reshape hours rather than cut across the board: take hours from Q3–Q4 stores and put them into Q1–Q2 produce and receiving

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Shrink sensitivity: FY2023–25 hours per $1,000 of sales −6.0% while shrink rose 0.5 pt, ≈ 0.083 pt per 1% fewer hours. This is a correlation (promotions and theft also moved), so we treat it as an estimate, not a proven cause.

slides.title: E-commerce loses ~$10M a year because 70% of its sales would have been made in stores anyway. Home delivery accounts for most of the loss

paragraphs.text: 1  WHY MARGIN FELL
E-commerce loses ~$10M a year because 70% of its sales would have been made in stores anyway. Home delivery accounts for most of the loss
Profit per order after fulfillment, FY2025, $
Why the loss grew, and what it means
•  Orders rose from 453k to 1,331k (FY2023–25) and the home-delivery share from 45% to 58%. Net fulfillment cost tripled, from $5.2M to $18.1M

•  Delivery economics got worse on both sides: the third-party cost per drop rose $12.90 → $13.80 while the average fee collected fell $3.40 → $3.10, because most baskets clear the $75 free-delivery threshold
•  Click-and-collect almost breaks even. Home delivery loses $12.34 an order
•  Freezing at current size (management’s draft) stops the loss growing but locks it in. The fix is the price and mix of delivery, not the volume
•  The owners want delivery kept, so we re-price it rather than close it. Exiting delivery would save more (~$8–10M) and is kept as a fallback

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Contribution per order = $96 basket × 30% incremental (survey: 70% would otherwise buy in store) × $0.20 contribution per new $ = $5.76. Fulfillment: picking $7.40 on every order; delivery $13.80 less fee $3.10 per delivered order (FY2025).

slides.title: The plan pulls four lever groups worth ~$29M a year by FY2028, net $22M after the 2027 wage step. Commercial levers carry nearly half

paragraphs.text: 2  WHAT TO DO
The plan pulls four lever groups worth ~$29M a year by FY2028, net $22M after the 2027 wage step. Commercial levers carry nearly half

data: Promo share 29% → 24% (FY2023 level) by cutting money-losing events; 70% realized after lost volume and targeted value reinvestment
Vendor share of markdowns 46% → 49% (FY2023: 55%); co-funding becomes a condition of each event
Share 18.5% → 20.5% (past pace +0.75 pt a year) at a +12-pt margin

Hold the rate flat at the 2026 renewal (provider asks +3%)

paragraphs.text: Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Levers are grouped by P&L line, so each one is counted once. Ratio-based levers are sized on the continuing-store sales base ($1,414.5M, i.e. FY2025 less closures plus 25% transfer). Evidence: H = tested or measured in the pack; M = derived from pack data; L = assumption-led.

slides.title: Commercial: cutting money-losing promotions, rebuilding vendor funding and growing private label are worth ~$14M a year

paragraphs.text: 2  WHAT TO DO
Commercial: cutting money-losing promotions, rebuilding vendor funding and growing private label are worth ~$14M a year
Cut loss-making promotions
Rebuild vendor funding
Grow private label
Sizing
Sizing
Sizing
•  Promo share 29% → 24%: −5 pts of sales moved to regular price
•  × 70% realization (lost incremental units, value reinvestment in ValuMart areas) = $6.9M
•  Removes ~45% of the ~11 pts of sales in money-losing events (38% of events)
•  Vendor share of markdowns 46% → 49% (+3 pts; FY2023 was 55%)
•  Least certain commercial lever: depends on negotiation
•  Below the FY2023–25 pace of +0.75 pt a year
How
How
How
•  Review every event after it runs; cut any event without a positive post-event return
•  Redeploy part of the savings to everyday value prices on key fresh items in ValuMart trade areas
•  No vendor co-funding, no event: make it a condition
•  Use the cut in event count as leverage in the annual vendor round
•  Lead the range in fresh, produce-adjacent and value tiers
•  Also answers the price-perception problem at a higher margin

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Vendor funding: promo sales $435.9M × 14-pt gap = $61.0M net give-up. At 54% borne by Harlow, gross markdowns ≈ $113M, so each 1 pt of vendor funding ≈ $1.13M (derived estimate; markdown spend is not reported directly).

slides.title: E-commerce: rolling out the tested delivery fee saves ~$2.5M a year and keeps delivery. The remaining ~$8M loss needs a second pricing step

paragraphs.text: 2  WHAT TO DO
E-commerce: rolling out the tested delivery fee saves ~$2.5M a year and keeps delivery. The remaining ~$8M loss needs a second pricing step
The e-commerce plan
•  Now: roll the $7.99 fee and $100 threshold out chain-wide. Small sales loss (−2%), with demand shifting to click-and-collect
•  2026 renewal: rebid the third-party contract and reject the +3% (worth $0.3M); each −10% on the rate ≈ $1.0M
•  FY2027: test a second pricing step (e.g. higher threshold or a delivery pass). The first test doubled the average fee yet lost only 9% of delivered orders
•  Steer growth to click-and-collect, which almost breaks even. Grow volume only where an order covers its fulfillment
•  Fallback: if delivery still loses >$6M a year by end-FY2027, the board revisits a slimmer delivery offer (option C, ~$8–10M)
Even after re-pricing, a delivered order still loses ~$9.04 ($5.76 contribution − $7.40 picking − $13.80 delivery + $6.40 fee). E-commerce will still lose ~$8M a year.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Fee test: 4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025. Results applied to FY2025 volumes. Lost contribution assumes all 2% of lost e-commerce sales leave Harlow (conservative; the survey suggests 70% would shift to stores).

slides.title: Store operations: moving hours into produce and receiving cuts shrink by ~$3.5M, and trimming overstaffed stores saves ~$2.8M

paragraphs.text: 2  WHAT TO DO
Store operations: moving hours into produce and receiving cuts shrink by ~$3.5M, and trimming overstaffed stores saves ~$2.8M
Shrink, FY2025, $M by cause
Reshape, don’t cut: the store-operations plan
•  Cancel the blanket 8% hours cut before it reaches the FY2026 schedules

•  Protect produce rotation and receiving checks in Q1–Q2 stores: fixed daily task hours that cannot be cut on busy days. Produce waste is the largest shrink cause, and fresh produce is the top reason to shop Harlow
•  Take hours from Q3–Q4 stores, where extra hours buy almost no shrink (0.1 pt between Q3 and Q4): −2% net chain hours, ≈ $3.6M gross, $3.0M after a shrink allowance
•  Theft (35% of shrink): target loss prevention at the highest-theft stores, funded from the capital envelope
•  Track weekly: shrink by store, checkout waits and on-shelf availability, as guard-rails on every hours change

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. Shrink $39.1M in FY2025 (2.6% × $1,503M): produce/fresh waste 45% ($17.6M), theft 35% ($13.7M), administrative and receiving errors 20% ($7.8M). Labor net saving = 2% × $181.9M − shrink allowance (2 × 0.083 pt × ¼ sensitivity × $1,503M), scaled to continuing stores.

slides.title: Portfolio: exiting the nine loss-making stores adds ~$6.6M a year. Six can close at lease expiry at no cost; three need a board vote and $7.5M

paragraphs.text: 2  WHAT TO DO
Portfolio: exiting the nine loss-making stores adds ~$6.6M a year. Six can close at lease expiry at no cost; three need a board vote and $7.5M

data: Sales moving to nearby Harlow stores (25%)

paragraphs.text: Recommendation
•  Six stores: serve notice now and exit at lease expiry, phased through FY2027. Range $3.0–5.4M if the transfer rate is 10–35%
•  Three stores: a two-quarter fix-or-exit plan, then a board vote in Q2 FY2027. Each year of delay costs ~$2.2M
•  Schedule exit costs after FY2026 so they do not hit the covenant year
•  Use the move of sales to nearby stores: target the 25% transfer with re-marketing and click-and-collect in the receiving stores
•  Closures reduce sales by ~$88M, so margin % rises faster than operating income

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis. The pack reports only combined figures for the nine stores, so we assume equal size (sales $13.1M, four-wall EBITDA −$0.34M each). The gain excludes the stores’ depreciation, which would also stop (conservative).

slides.title: FY2026: the fastest levers lift operating income to ~$25M, clearing the $20M covenant. A downside contingency is pre-agreed

paragraphs.text: 3  WHAT IT DELIVERS
FY2026: the fastest levers lift operating income to ~$25M, clearing the $20M covenant. A downside contingency is pre-agreed
FY2026 operating income, $M (covenant minimum $20M)
Covenant $20M
Pre-agreed contingency if Q2 run-rate < $22M
•  Bring the second delivery-pricing step forward (+$1–2M)
•  Cut the next tranche of money-losing events (the other ~55% of their volume)

The low case (≈$19.3M) and management’s draft after its shrink effect (≈$19.8M) both fall just short of the covenant. Hence the contingency.

slides.title: We ask the board for four decisions today

paragraphs.text: 4  WHAT TO DO FIRST
We ask the board for four decisions today

Four lever groups, ~$29M a year by FY2028. Target 3.0% operating margin, with a base case of 2.65% and a named stretch plan. The blanket 8% hours cut is withdrawn.

slides.title: Appendix: how the key figures were calculated

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
Appendix: how the key figures were calculated

Margin bridge. Each cost line’s % of sales in FY2025 minus FY2023. Gross profit 26.04% → 25.02% (−1.02 pts); e-commerce 0.37% → 1.20% (+0.84); labor 11.80% → 12.10% (+0.30); occupancy 5.80% → 6.00% (+0.20); other SG&A 4.70% → 4.70%.
Gross-margin split. Promo: (29.0 − 24.0) × 14 pts = −0.70 pts. Private label: (18.5 − 17.0) × 12 pts = +0.18. Shrink: 2.6 − 2.1 = −0.50. Total −1.02 pts. $ values at FY2025 sales of $1,503M.
Labor. Hours = 6.60 × 1,503 = 9.92M (FY2025) vs 7.02 × 1,420 = 9.97M (FY2023). Cost = hours × wage (reconciles to $181.9M / $167.6M within rounding).
Vendor funding. Net promo give-up 14% × $435.9M = $61.0M = 54% of gross markdowns, so gross ≈ $113M and 1 pt of funding ≈ $1.13M.

E-commerce. Sales 1,331k × $96 = $127.8M. Incremental contribution 30% × 20% × $127.8M = $7.7M. Net fulfillment $18.1M (picking 1,331k × $7.40 + delivery 772k × $13.80 − fees 772k × $3.10). Net = −$10.4M.
Fee rollout. Delivered 772k × 0.91 = 703k; click-and-collect 559k × 1.14 = 637k. New net fulfillment $15.1M (saving $3.0M). Lost contribution 2% × $127.8M × 20% = $0.5M. Net +$2.5M.
Stores. Per store: sales $13.1M, EBITDA −$0.34M. Gain = EBITDA avoided + sales × 25% × 12%. Six: 2.07 + 2.36 = $4.43M; three: 1.03 + 1.18 = $2.21M.
FY2028 base. Ratio levers × 0.941 (continuing-sales factor). Margin = $37.5M ÷ $1,411.9M sales (FY2025 less $88.5M net closure loss less $2.6M e-commerce) = 2.65%.
Wage step. 4% × $181.9M × 0.941 = −$6.85M (assumes the rise flows through the whole pay scale).
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis.

slides.title: Appendix: key assumptions and judgment calls made without management input

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
